study_identification_part.si4_title: Shared differential factors underlying individual spontaneous neural activity abnormalities in major depressive disorder

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To identify shared differential factors underlying individual-specific spontaneous neural activity abnormalities in major depressive disorder (MDD) using normative modeling and non-negative matrix factorization, and to explore their neurobiological relevance and clinical applications for subtyping depression.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: The study used multiple statistical approaches: (1) Two-sided two-sample t-tests controlling for age, sex, site, and mean FD to examine group-level differences between patients and HCs with FDR correction; (2) Multilinear regression models to test associations between differential factors and group-level abnormalities, evaluated with permutation testing (10,000 permutations); (3) Two-sample t-tests (controlling for age, sex, site, mean FD) with FDR correction to compare factor compositions between clinical subgroups (treated vs untreated, first-episode vs recurrent, female vs male); (4) Pearson's correlation coefficients with FDR correction to assess relationships between factor compositions and clinical features (HAMD scores, illness duration, age of onset, mean FD); (5) Spatial correlations with FDR correction to examine consistency of differential factors across subgroups and datasets (Hungarian matching algorithm used for factor correspondence); (6) Non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) to decompose individualized Z-scores into differential factors, with generalizability error (GE) metric to determine optimal number of factors; (7) Linear regression to quantify variance explained by differential factors in individualized abnormalities, with permutation testing (10,000 times) to assess significance; (8) Multilinear models with permutation testing (10,000 times) and FDR correction to link differential factors to neurotransmitter receptor/transporter profiles; dominance analysis to determine relative importance of predictors; (9) Pearson's correlations with permutation testing (10,000 times) and FDR correction to assess associations between differential factors and inflammation-related gene expression profiles; (10) Gaussian mixture model (GMM) with Bayesian information criterion (BIC) for subtyping based on factor compositions; (11) Adjusted Rand index (ARI) to assess stability and replicability of subtypes across datasets; (12) Two-tailed two-sample t-tests with Bonferroni correction to characterize ALFF differences for each subtype vs HCs; (13) Permutation tests (10,000 times) to identify putative disease epicenters for each differential factor based on structural covariance network rankings.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Four robust and reproducible differential factors (two positive, two negative) were identified that underlie individual-specific ALFF abnormalities in MDD, accounting for 57.19% of variance; these factors explained group-level abnormalities, showed distinct associations with neurotransmitter systems and inflammation-related genes, and enabled identification of four distinct MDD subtypes with unique ALFF patterns and clinical features.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The study identified four differential factors (two positive and two negative) underlying individualized ALFF abnormalities in MDD across two large multi-center datasets (2424 MDD patients, 2183 HCs). These factors accounted for 57.19% (±6.84%) of variance in individualized abnormalities (permutation p < 1.00×10⁻⁴) and explained 71% (discovery) and 68% (validation) of group-level ALFF abnormalities (both adjusted R² with permutation p < 1.00×10⁻⁴). The factors showed high spatial correlations between datasets: r=77.28×10⁻² for positive factor 1, r=84.98×10⁻² for positive factor 2, r=66.66×10⁻² for negative factor 1, and r=80.38×10⁻² for negative factor 2 (all FDR-corrected p < 1.00×10⁻⁴). Cross-dataset validation showed factors identified in one dataset explained 52% and 46% of group-level abnormalities in the other dataset (both permutation p < 1.00×10⁻⁴). Clinical associations revealed: recurrent patients had significantly lower weights of negative factor 1 than first-episode patients (t=-3.77, Cohen's d=-0.46, FDR-corrected p=0.07×10⁻²); treated patients showed significantly lower weights of positive factors (t=-2.49, Cohen's d=-0.18, FDR-corrected p=1.74×10⁻² for positive factor 1; t=-2.12, Cohen's d=-0.15, FDR-corrected p=3.46×10⁻² for positive factor 2) and higher weights of negative factors (t=5.21, Cohen's d=0.38 for negative factor 1; t=5.23, Cohen's d=0.38 for negative factor 2; both FDR-corrected p < 1.00×10⁻⁴) compared to untreated patients; HAMD scores correlated positively with positive factor weights (r=14.41×10⁻² and 12.21×10⁻², FDR-corrected p < 0.04×10⁻²) and negatively with negative factor weights (r=-11.22×10⁻² and -9.58×10⁻², FDR-corrected p < 0.53×10⁻²). Neurobiological correlates included: neurotransmitter receptor/transporter distributions explained 52%, 78%, 32%, and 76% of variance in the four factors respectively (all FDR-corrected permutation p < 1.00×10⁻⁴), with M1, DAT, and A4B2 receptors showing particular importance via dominance analysis; inflammation-related gene expression correlated significantly with positive factor 2 (r=-29.07×10⁻², FDR-corrected permutation p < 1.00×10⁻⁴) and negative factor 2 (r=-37.96×10⁻², FDR-corrected permutation p < 1.00×10⁻⁴); all four factors were informed by structural covariance networks (r=22.37×10⁻² to 46.06×10⁻², FDR-corrected p < 0.001) with distinct epicenters identified for each factor (all permutation p < 0.05). Factor compositions enabled identification of four reproducible subtypes with distinct patterns: subtype 1 showed overall decreased ALFF, subtype 2 showed overall increased ALFF, subtype 3 showed increased ALFF in putamen/striatum but decreased in visual cortex (calcarine, lingual, cuneus), and subtype 4 showed modest increases in inferior temporal gyrus, parahippocampus, middle and inferior frontal gyrus. Cross-dataset validation showed good stability (ARI=0.52 for validation-to-discovery prediction, ARI=0.39 for discovery-to-validation prediction). All major findings were successfully replicated in the independent validation dataset despite different acquisition equipment, protocols, and preprocessing strategies.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Insufficient clinical information (symptom dimensions, comorbidities); lack of quantitative analysis of medication effects (types, doses); cross-sectional design limits insights into evolution of differential factors with disease progression
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: First, we did not have sufficient clinical information, such as symptom dimensions and comorbidities. The exploration of whether the identified differential factors correspond to specific symptom dimensions and are influenced by comorbidities warrants investigation in future research. Second, while significant differences in factor compositions associated with medication were observed, a quantitative analysis of the relationship between changes in factor compositions and medication variables, such as types and doses, was not conducted. Third, the inclusion of only cross-sectional data in our study restricts insights into the evolution of differential factors with disease progression. Future investigations should explore how these factors evolve over time to enhance our understanding of their dynamic nature.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study introduces a novel dimensional framework for understanding heterogeneity in MDD by decomposing individualized ALFF abnormalities into shared differential factors using non-negative matrix factorization (NMF). This approach reconciles the contradiction between extensive individual variability and phenotypic similarities among patients. The validation strategy was particularly robust, using two large independent multi-center datasets (34 total sites) with different acquisition equipment, protocols, preprocessing strategies, and medication statuses. The study performed comprehensive biological validation by linking factors to neurotransmitter systems (using PET-derived receptor maps from 1238 healthy individuals across 19 neurotransmitter receptors/transporters), gene expression profiles (using AHBA data for 14 inflammation-related genes), and structural covariance networks (using independent SALD dataset with 492 healthy individuals aged 19-80). The identification of distinct epicenters for each factor aligns with network-based spreading hypotheses of psychiatric disorders. The subtyping approach based on factor compositions revealed patterns not evident in traditional group-level analyses, such as the widespread ALFF increase in subtype 2. Normative model performance was extensively validated using 10-fold CV (100 repetitions), leave-one-site-out CV, and cross-dataset validation, demonstrating robust generalizability. The study also validated results using a different brain atlas (AAL with 90 regions) in addition to the primary brain connectome atlas (246 regions).

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study represents a comprehensive investigation of heterogeneity in spontaneous neural activity abnormalities in MDD using normative modeling. The large sample sizes (2424 MDD patients, 2183 HCs across 34 sites in two independent datasets: DIDA-MDD with 9 sites and REST-meta-MDD with 25 sites) and extensive validation strategies provide strong evidence for the robustness of findings. The study is notable for: (1) thorough validation of GPR performance using multiple strategies including 10-fold CV repeated 100 times, leave-one-site-out CV, cross-dataset validation (training on one dataset and testing on the other), and validation with different brain atlases (brain connectome atlas with 246 regions and AAL with 90 regions); (2) replication of all major findings in an independent validation dataset with different acquisition equipment (3.0-T GE vs Siemens scanners), protocols, and preprocessing strategies (EPI template vs DARTEL normalization, different smoothing approaches); (3) integration of multiple levels of analysis from individual Z-score deviations to differential factors (via NMF) to subtypes (via GMM); (4) multimodal biological validation using neurotransmitter receptor/transporter maps (PET-derived atlas from 1238 healthy individuals covering 19 receptors/transporters across 9 neurotransmitter systems), inflammation-related gene expression profiles (AHBA data for 14 genes), and structural covariance networks (from independent SALD dataset with 492 healthy individuals aged 19-80). There are apparent reporting inconsistencies in age standard deviations: main text reports discovery HC SD as 19.25 years while Table S1 shows 13.87 years; validation HC SD is reported as 24.552 or 245.52 years which is clearly erroneous. Similar inconsistencies exist for MDD age SDs. Discovery dataset included both first-episode (n=512) and recurrent (n=79) patients, as well as medicated (n=277) and unmedicated (n=622) patients. Validation dataset included first-episode (n=538) and recurrent (n=282) patients, as well as medicated (n=408) and unmedicated (n=447) patients. The four identified differential factors showed reproducible spatial patterns across datasets and clinical subgroups, with differential factors explaining substantial variance in both individualized abnormalities and group-level patterns. The four subtypes showed distinct clinical profiles and ALFF patterns, with good cross-dataset stability (ARI values of 0.39-0.52). Software used: DPARSF v5.4 for ALFF calculation, GAUSSIAN PROCESS REGRESSION AND CLASSIFICATION Toolbox v4.2 for normative modeling, scikit-learn v1.3.0 for NMF.
